title: How much of your money to bet?
hook: A coin favours you 60/40. Does betting a bigger share of your money grow it faster?

knows: a favourable bet wins more often than it loses
gains and losses on a share of your money multiply
doesNotKnow: that there is a best stake for a favourable bet
that staking more than it shrinks the typical result

misconception: With a favourable bet, staking more of your money each round always grows it faster.
objective: The learner can explain that because a loss at a large stake costs more than a win regains (1.6 x 0.4 = 0.64), the middle player's money grows fastest at a 20% stake and shrinks at 60%, even though every bet favours them.
keyState: Seen stakes 20% (middle player x7.49) and 60% (x0.00021, 1 of 31 above start).

claims.text: On the stage's 31 players the middle player ends 100 rounds with x2.40 at a 5% stake, x4.50 at 10%, x7.49 at 20%, x4.37 at 30%, x0.78 at 40% and x0.00021 at 60%.
claims.source: flips(), middle(), path() in src/demos/probability/bet-too-much-and-go-broke/model.ts, mulberry32 seed 2, CHOSEN: the first seed whose middle player has exactly 60 heads, the median over seeds (seed 60, tried first, gave 57 heads and x2.46 at 10% vs x2.22 at 20%, i.e. 10% best for that run). Over seeds 1-1000 the middle player's heads had middle 95% 58-62, and 20% was the best of the original five stakes for the middle player in 982 of 1000 seeds (the 30% stake was added in v2; growth per round at 30% is 0.0147, below 20%'s 0.0201). With 60 heads these values equal the exact typical result e^(100 g(f)).

claims.text: Players above their start after 100 rounds: 31, 30, 27, 21, 13 and 1 of 31 at stakes 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, 40%, 60%.
claims.source: above() in Demo.tsx over the seed-2 sample (c1); one chosen sample, not a rate.

claims.text: At a 60% stake a win multiplies your money by 1.6 and a loss by 0.4, so one win then one loss leaves 1.6 x 0.4 = 0.64 of your money; the stage prints this for every stake.
claims.source: Arithmetic; order does not matter (0.4 x 1.6 is the same).

claims.text: The share that grows money fastest is 2 x 0.6 - 1 = 20% (the Kelly rule), for this model coin; real bets differ.
claims.source: Typical growth per round g(f) = 0.6 ln(1+f) + 0.4 ln(1-f), maximised at f* = 2p - 1 (growth() in model.ts: 0.0088, 0.0150, 0.0201, -0.0024, -0.0845). Kelly, J. L. (1956), 'A New Interpretation of Information Rate', Bell System Technical Journal 35: 917-926.

claims.text: The middle player is the one half the players do better than and half worse; with the same coin flips at every stake it is the same player throughout.
claims.source: Final money (1+f)^H (1-f)^(100-H) increases with heads H for any f in (0,1), so ranking by heads ranks by money at every stake; middle() picks the 16th of 31.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: a made-up coin that lands heads 60% of the time and pays even money, one fixed stake share each round. It is not advice for real bets or markets.
claims.source: Reveal line 'for this model coin; real bets differ. Not advice.'

recall.question: A bet wins 70% of the time at even money. A friend stakes 80% of their money every round. Will they typically get rich?
options: No, the stake is far above the best share of 40%
Only if they play more rounds
recall.why: The best share is 2 x 0.7 - 1 = 40%. At 80% one win and one loss leave 1.8 x 0.2 = 0.36, so the typical player shrinks, and more rounds make it worse.
